When he first started to quarantine with his family, Michael Alexander, an insurance consultant in Houston, Texas, was trying to remain hopeful. He and his wife were working from home while caring for their 2-year-old, and a new baby was on the way.
“The first week you think you’ll find a way a way to make life continue,” said Alexander, 42. “But then you have a child with certain nap times who needs a certain lunch, you’ve got a dog barking, you’ve got a kid crying, you’re trying to be on a business call — I just gave up.”
Then after his wife gave birth, their household, he said, plunged into chaos. “That’s when I was like, I’m not an insurance professional anymore,” he said. “I’m a caregiver, and I do insurance work on the side.”
Increasingly desperate as what he calls “two months of grief” stretched into the summer months, Alexander enrolled his kids in a local day care open to children of essential workers. He worries about potential virus exposure, particularly for his newborn and his wife, who has an underlying health condition. At dropoff, he sees some parents not a wearing mask and it fills him with rage. But a worse outcome, he said, would be losing his business. “We tried to settle on the bad and not the catastrophic decision.”
Parents across the country who are dealing with similar situations are
facing potential burnout
. Farhad Manjoo wrote
a column on the subject
in April, and over
1,000 readers
had stories to share — about taking care of children with special needs, crying in front of the kids and searching for a single moment of solitude. And that was
before
school ended. As summer break kicks off, we wanted to know how they’re faring now. Here’s what eight families had to say.
She’s grateful for the break.
Nicole Sutton, 44, Tampa, Fla.
Nicole Sutton, 44, needed absolute quiet to concentrate on a three-hour-long certification exam for her graduate program in public health. So she took the test at a time when she knew her 4-year-old son wouldn’t be making noise: 4 a.m.
Sutton, a single parent who also lives with and takes care of her mother, struggled throughout her spring semester to study while managing online preschool classes and learning assignments. Nic, her son, is hyperactive, she said, and was cut off from the community services and regular home visits that typically helped support him. Sutton would do her schoolwork after putting Nic to bed; she averaged only three to four hours of sleep each night. Her job, at the school where she attends, had to be dropped: “There’s no way right now I can do more than what I’m doing,” she said.
While Sutton’s taking classes over the summer, she’s grateful her son’s school is finished. “It was more stressful than it was helpful,” she said. “I think I cried every single day.” She plans to spend the summer doing more activities that use up his energy during the day: mountain biking, hiking, baking…
They formed a “pod.”
Vanessa and Liam Nelson, 44 and 43, respectively, Petaluma, Calif.
“After school ended, everyone was like, what do we do?” said Vanessa Nelson, 44, who lives with her husband, Liam, and their 9- and 5-year-old kids. Just a few weeks into distance learning, after struggling to balance both their work and watching the kids, Vanessa lost her job at an engineering firm. In some ways, she said, the layoff was a relief; she primarily watched the kids during the day, while Liam continued to work from home.
But they wanted to fill the void of unstructured time during summer, so they recently formed a
“quarantine pod”
with a family who lives down the street. They play tennis together, carefully marking which ball belongs to which family, and they devise scavenger hunts for each other. Vanessa said she also gets to take breaks from the kids by going for walks with the mom from the other family.
In turn, they do decline invites for the kids to play with families outside of the pod. Liam’s mother lives in a cottage house behind the Nelson’s home, and they want to minimize the risk of potentially exposing her to the virus. “It feels like being back in high school,” Vanessa said. “Like, ‘oh, we can’t hang out with you?’”
They’re fostering childhood independence.
Cambria Bojorquez, 43, Long Beach, Calif.
In some ways, many of the parents interviewed for this story said that the pandemic has granted their kids more autonomy, and they expect summer break to be a boon for their independence. Cambria Bojorquez, 43 and a doctor, said she lets her 11-, 9-, and 6-year-old ride bikes around the neighborhood while she’s at the hospital and her husband works at home. They head to the park or coast near the beach. “I worry about their boredom,” she said. “But boredom’s easier than schooling.”
Erika Beers, 37, York, Penn.
“It’s “Lord of the Flies” over here,” said Erika Beers, 37. She works remotely for a start-up while caring for her three kids — ages 3, 6, and 8 — during the day. Her husband, a power lineman, is out in the field all day and sometimes has to travel overnight. Beers brings her laptop outside and tries to monitor her kids while they play on a backyard waterslide and obstacle courses she sets up for them. Her oldest child has autism, and the lack of structure in their days can be particularly challenging for her. Mornings, Beers said, are especially difficult: “Every morning I get up and I’m like, ‘Okay, we’re going to be ready and working at 9:30.’ Then 11 gets here and I’m like, ‘Oh my god, you’re still not wearing your socks — just one person get dressed!’”
They’re wondering what happens after parental leave.
Katie Church, 30, Rural Maine
For the bulk of shelter in place, Katie Church, 30, was caring for her 3.5-year-old daughter while working remotely and getting ready to give birth. Her husband was putting in long hours at a local grocery store, as well as taking on shifts as a volunteer firefighter. They have a short six weeks of parental leave together now that the baby is here. But Church is already anxious about how she’ll manage with a baby and a toddler when he goes back to work. She’d already struggled with just one to look after.
“The mute button on Zoom became my new best friend,” Church said. “It reached a point where I just gave up.” She saved envelopes filled with crafts that her grandmother sends each week to occupy her daughter during important meetings: popsicle-stick puppets, or templates for coloring pages filled with families. Each drawing of a family Church’s grandmother has sent features a little sister. Now, her toddler is adjusting to having the real thing.
Nicholas Wright, 35, Brooklyn
Many parents expressed the sense of time slipping away suddenly, entire hours seeming to pass without notice. When Nicholas Wright, his wife, and their toddler and newborn left their apartment in Park Slope for his mom’s house in New Jersey, he said it felt like being in “this weird temporal reality.” Wright, 35, works remotely as an architect; his wife goes back to work from maternity leave next week. The two are already so exhausted they can barely make it through half a Netflix episode at night, he said, and they worry about what will happen when they’re both working full-time.
“Everything’s blurring together,” he said. “People say, ‘it’s the summer,’ and I’m like, ‘I guess so.’”
